comment: target = the law's threshold; limit = current ratchet (worst allowed). Tighten limits as recommendations land; never loosen without review. Timing limits are generous regression guards for a shared PC, not benchmarks.
calibration: Deterministic budgets (geometry, counts, KLM model time, axe, focus): limit = the value measured on the snapshot machine (docs/hci/report.snapshot.json, Windows, Chrome 154), plus at most a little headroom where fonts or the Chrome version could shift geometry. Wall-clock budgets: a median guard (doherty.settled_p50, target = limit = 400 ms; measured about 60 ms) plus a loose tail guard (doherty.settled_p95, limit 4000 ms; the same UI gave 1.4 to 2.5 s p95 over several runs, single samples up to 4.5 s), because this PC is shared and noisy. Timing budgets catch order-of-magnitude regressions; they are not benchmarks. Re-derive the limits when the machine, Chrome or the UI changes.

budgets.note: Chrome-build and font specific: five moves sit between 4.0 and 4.4 bits, so the limit is 1 above the measured 6 to avoid failing on a one-pixel layout difference; centre-landing convention (see nearest-edge variant)
measured 4.405 bits; geometry is Chrome-build and font specific
modelled, not measured: a regression guard on the journey definition (measured model value 62.7 s), so adding a journey step trips it on purpose; no law defines a threshold, so target = limit
first DOM mutation after the click (JavaScript-task latency, excludes paint); passes trivially, it is not perceived latency
median over all interactions and repeats; robust to load spikes, so it is the timing regression guard
wall-clock on a shared PC; p95 varied between about 1.4 and 2.5 s across runs under different load, the ratchet is generous on purpose
count of violating axe rules (integer), measured 1
